title: The Story of a Bondi Beach Icon: Olga Colavecchio
author: Beach Volleyball TV
imageAlt: Olga Colavecchio on the sand at Bondi Beach
excerpt: Every beach has its legends. At Bondi, few are as recognisable as Olga Colavecchio — and now she’s telling her story.

content.text: Spend enough mornings on the sand at Bondi and you’ll come to know the regulars — the people who make a beach feel like a community. Olga Colavecchio is one of them, and her story is woven into the fabric of Bondi beach volleyball.
We sat down with Olga for one of our favourite films of the year. It’s a celebration of a life lived by the water, and a reminder of why so many of us fell in love with this game.

title: Sand, Salt and 6am Starts: Meet the Sunrise Crew
author: Beach Volleyball TV
imageAlt: Morning sun over calm waves washing onto the sand
excerpt: Before most of Sydney is awake, the nets are up at North Bondi. Here’s why the early session has become the heart of our community.

content.text: There is a particular kind of quiet on Bondi at 5:45am. The water is glassy, the ocean pool swimmers are already out, and a small group is unrolling court lines on the sand at the north end.

Our Wednesday Sunrise Social Sessions started as a handful of friends looking for a game before work. Today they’re the easiest way into the Beach Volleyball TV community — free, friendly and open to anyone who can make it down by six.
How it works
Courts go up at first light and games run on a rolling rotation.
Players are grouped by level so every game is competitive and fun.
Nets and balls are provided — just bring water and sunscreen.
Coffee afterwards is optional, but highly recommended.
You come for the volleyball. You stay because of the people.
If you’ve been meaning to try beach volleyball, this is your sign. Check the
Events page
for the next session and come say g’day.

title: Two Sydney 2000 Olympians on Coaching the Next Generation
author: Beach Volleyball TV

excerpt: Matt Grinlaubs and Angela Clarke Gaviglio both represented Australia at Sydney 2000. Today they’re shaping the players who come next.

content.text: In 2000, beach volleyball came to Bondi on the biggest stage of all. Two of the Australians who competed at those home Games are still giving back to the sport — this time from the coaching side of the court.

Sydney 2000 Olympian Matt Grinlaubs is the owner of Sandstorm and a coach to players at every level. We caught up with him to talk about his career and what he looks for in the athletes he works with.

title: Brooke Ronan and the Road to Brisbane 2032
author: Beach Volleyball TV
imageAlt: Title card for Brooke Ronan: My 2032 Olympic Dream
excerpt: A home Olympics is coming to Brisbane in 2032. For Brooke Ronan, that date is more than a headline — it’s the goal.

content.text: When the Olympic Games come to Brisbane in 2032, it will be the first home Games since Sydney 2000 — when Bondi Beach hosted the beach volleyball. For a generation of Australian players, that date has become a north star.
Brooke Ronan is one of them. She sat down with Beach Volleyball TV to talk about her Olympic dream and what it will take to get there.

title: Five Drills to Sharpen Your Beach Defence This Summer
author: Beach Volleyball TV
imageAlt: A volleyball resting in churned-up sand next to the court line
excerpt: Defence wins points on sand. Five simple drills you can run with a partner to read hitters earlier and dig more balls.

content.text: In beach volleyball there are only two of you covering the whole court, so every dig matters. The good news: defence is one of the most trainable skills in the game. Here are five drills to take to your next session.
1. Read and react

Your partner stands on a box or the net side and hits controlled shots to your left, right or short. Call the shot out loud the moment you read it, before the ball is struck. Reading early beats moving fast.
2. Sprawl and recover
Start low, take a tossed ball to either side with a sprawl, then get back to your base position before the next toss. Ten reps each side, rest, repeat. Recovery speed is half of defence.
3. Pokey and cut shot coverage
Have your partner mix hard-driven balls with cut shots and pokies. Your job: hold your base until the hitter commits. It trains patience, which is the hardest defensive skill of all.
4. Dig to target
Place a towel two metres off the net in the middle of the court. Every dig should land near it. A dig your partner can set is worth twice as much as one that simply stays up.
5. Transition finish
Finish every defensive rep by transitioning to attack. Dig, move to your approach, hit. Defence only becomes points if you can turn it into offence.
Reading early beats moving fast.
